title: When No One is Listening
html:
If you want to teach, you need an audience. But you shouldn’t expect people to listen until you have:

  1. Done the things that you’re preaching, and…

  2. Had exceptional outcomes,

If you haven’t done these things, people won’t care. And, frankly, they probably shouldn’t.

When presented with new ideas, it’s natural for us apes to evaluate them using proxies such as the authority, status, or success of the person sharing them, rather than evaluating them from first principles. For example, if a broke ten-year-old has a finance blog and tells people to start investing in low-risk, steady-growth options and let the market make them rich over time, no one would listen. But when Warren Buffett says the same thing, people start dumping money into the market. Why? Because he’s Warren effin’ Buffet.

In domains with clear metrics of success—like investing, sports, etc.—it’s easy to see who’s on top and worth paying attention to. But in the practical philosophy space—or “self-help”🤢, as some call it—success isn’t well-defined, and sussing out who’s worth paying attention to is hard. What's obvious, though, is that age is often used as a proxy for wisdom. This makes sense, of course, because the wisest are often the oldest; we use the term “elder” for a reason. However, being elderly doesn’t necessarily make you an elder; it just makes you old. And just as being elderly doesn’t guarantee wisdom, being young doesn’t guarantee a lack thereof. Still, it’s entirely reasonable for young whippersnappers like myself not to be listened to or taken seriously. After all, wise people are painfully rare, and most of them are old(ish), so for someone to be both young and wise is rarer still.

Now, am I claiming to be wise? Not quite. I’ve certainly been called worse. But I don’t think it’s arrogant of me to claim that I’ve grappled more with the question “How do I live a good life?” than the average Zoomer. So, while I might not have much to offer the Boomers in terms of insight, I think I have at least something to offer someone. And I don’t think they’re listening.

But is it so bad to be living and writing in obscurity at 24 years old?

At this point in my life, not having a large audience is a gift. I can write (almost) without consequence—strengthening my thinking and writing—and give myself an outlet through which to process life—all with the humility of knowing that, regularly, my thinking will suck, my writing will suck, and I’ll be so embarrassed by past work that I’ll want to take it down. But I won’t, as the failures will act as a chronicle of growth, not only as a writer, but as a person.

When no one is listening, I write as an offering—to encourage the unlikely event that my word-vomit might find the right person—at the right time—and make a difference. One day, I hope to be lucky enough that, if ever someone decides to listen, I can make them feel empowered, curious, and, most importantly, less alone.

I think you should publish your writing too :)
